clinical_category: Postoperative lung-expansion care - appropriate role of incentive spirometry
blueprint_topic: Comfort-supportive respiratory care and multimodal postoperative pulmonary-complication prevention
stem: A postoperative client has an order that includes incentive spirometry. Which nursing plan is most consistent with current AARC guidance?

options.A: Use incentive spirometry as one component of care along with deep-breathing techniques, directed coughing, early mobilization, and adequate pain control
options.B: Use incentive spirometry alone as the routine prophylactic intervention and omit other postoperative pulmonary measures
options.C: Keep the client on bed rest so incentive spirometry can replace early mobilization
options.D: Avoid deep-breathing exercises because they provide no comparable postoperative benefit

rationale: A is correct. The AARC incentive-spirometry guideline states that incentive spirometry alone is not recommended for routine preoperative or postoperative prevention of pulmonary complications. When incentive spirometry is used, AARC recommends combining it with deep-breathing techniques, directed coughing, early mobilization, and optimal analgesia. The guideline also notes that deep-breathing exercises may provide similar benefit to incentive spirometry in the perioperative setting. B incorrectly treats incentive spirometry as a stand-alone routine prophylaxis. C contradicts the recommendation for early mobilization. D contradicts the guideline's recognition of deep-breathing benefit.
educational_objective: Use incentive spirometry, when ordered for postoperative care, as an adjunct within a multimodal lung-expansion strategy rather than as a stand-alone replacement for deep breathing, coughing, mobilization, and adequate analgesia.
source_document_title: Incentive Spirometry: 2011 — AARC Clinical Practice Guideline; AARC Clinical Practice Guideline: Effectiveness of Nonpharmacologic Airway Clearance Therapies in Hospitalized Patients
source_version_date: Incentive Spirometry guideline published 2011 and still listed by AARC in 2026 as an Expert Panel Reference-Based Guideline, not retired; postoperative airway-clearance guideline published 2013 and current on AARC guideline resources at access 2026-08-18
source_locator: AARC 'Incentive Spirometry: 2011' → Recommendations 14.1–14.5: incentive spirometry alone is not recommended for routine pre/postoperative prevention; when used, combine with deep breathing, directed coughing, early mobilization, and optimal analgesia; deep-breathing exercises may provide the same perioperative benefit; routine use to prevent atelectasis after upper-abdominal surgery or CABG is not recommended. AARC guideline index → Incentive Spirometry (2011) remains listed under Expert Panel Reference-Based Guidelines. 2013 nonpharmacologic airway-clearance guideline → postoperative recommendations: routine prophylactic incentive spirometry is not recommended; early mobility/ambulation is recommended.
source_claim_supported: Current AARC guideline resources directly support incentive spirometry only as part of a broader postoperative respiratory-care strategy and reject routine stand-alone prophylactic use.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort client-needs subcategory (6–12% of items), within Physiological Integrity; this item tests supportive postoperative respiratory care, mobility, pain control, and comfort measures that promote effective breathing and recovery.
correction_summary: Total clinical rebuild. The source item implied that routine incentive spirometry itself prevents postoperative atelectasis and complications. Current AARC guidance explicitly rejects stand-alone routine prophylactic use. The final item tests the guideline-supported multimodal approach and preserves incentive spirometry only as an adjunct when ordered.
audit_findings: The original item's claim that routine incentive spirometry helps prevent postoperative atelectasis was too broad and conflicts with the AARC recommendation against stand-alone routine prophylactic use.
AARC currently lists the 2011 incentive-spirometry guideline as active reference guidance rather than retired.
The exact recommendations support combining incentive spirometry with deep breathing, coughing, early mobilization, and adequate analgesia when it is used.
Distractors test the specific errors of stand-alone use, bed rest, and rejection of deep breathing; none is defensible under the guideline.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct answer, no unsupported frequency prescription, no second answer, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
